items.label: International Patient Summary
items.short_def: An internationally agreed minimum summary of a person's health (problems, medicines, allergies and more) designed to be read in any system or country.
items.long_def: The International Patient Summary is a content specification (HL7 FHIR IPS implementation guide, aligned with ISO 27269) that defines the essential clinical facts needed for unplanned or cross-border care. In this workshop it is offered as a use case that continues the Day 1 work: teams trace what a summary needs from the Client Registry, Lifelong Health Record, Terminology Service and trust services in order to move between facilities or countries. The RA names the IPS as the kind of shared, internationally aligned specification that cross-border exchange depends on, alongside a trust framework and an explicit legal basis.
items.examples: Outer-island referral to the national hospital; overseas medical referral; patient summary exchange between EU countries (MyHealth@EU); summary carried by a traveller or migrant worker
items.source: HL7 International (FHIR IPS IG); RA 1.2.2 (Box 1.3); RA 3.6.4; Bootcamp Day 1

items.label: Immunisation
items.short_def: Every vaccination is recorded once and available wherever the person is seen next, so schedules, coverage and outbreaks can be tracked.
items.long_def: Immunisation is a common first use case because it touches the core registries: the Client Registry to know who each child or adult is, the Facility and Health Workforce Registries for where and by whom the dose was given, and the Product Registry for which vaccine and batch. The RA uses the example of a birth recorded once so that both civil registration and the electronic immunisation registry can act on it. Shared records support reminders for missed doses, coverage reporting, and digital vaccination certificates that can be verified across borders.
items.examples: Electronic immunisation registry (EIR); digital vaccination certificates verified through the WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN); SMART Guidelines for immunisation
items.source: RA 3.6.3; Appendix E (Goals 3 and 7); WHO SMART Guidelines

items.label: Trusted data foundations
items.short_def: Core health data is captured once and reused reliably across programmes, services and levels of care.
items.long_def: Goal 1 aims to end the re-entry of the same people, facility, workforce and product data in many separate programme systems. The RA treats it as the foundation for the other six goals rather than a goal with its own mapping: every other goal reuses the same client, facility and workforce registries, Terminology Service, Product Registry and Lifelong Health Record. Choosing it in the workshop means focusing on those shared, well-governed reference data and their stewardship, which the RA describes as the REDDHI minimum core.
items.examples: Stop re-entering the same patient and facility data in many programme systems; one master facility list used by HMIS, supply chain and surveillance; programme reports generated from data already captured at the point of care

items.label: Capable, well-distributed workforce
items.short_def: Health workers are identifiable and verifiable, deployed where they are needed, paid reliably and supported to keep their skills current.
items.long_def: Goal 2 needs an authoritative record of who each health worker is, their occupation, registration and licence status, so that clinical, payroll, financing and regulatory systems can rely on it. The RA centres this goal on the Health Workforce Registry, supported by the Terminology Service for occupation and qualification coding and the Health Facility Registry to link workers to where they practise. Payroll, HR information systems and training-tracking tools sit outside DPI-H and consume the registry; the goal adds no new DPI-H component.
items.examples: National register of licensed health workers linked to deployment and payroll; licence verification by a facility or insurer; mapping staff shortages by district
items.source: RA 1.5.1; Appendix E (Goal 2); Appendix C (Health Workforce Registry)

items.label: Quality & continuity of care
items.short_def: Care that draws on a person's full history, follows current evidence at the point of care and is coordinated across providers.
items.long_def: Goal 3 asks the system to assemble a person's longitudinal record from many places of care, put current computable guidance in front of health workers, and coordinate referrals, transitions and follow-up. It rests mostly on shared components other goals already need: Client Registry, workforce and facility registries, Terminology Service and the Lifelong Health Record. The one new DPI-H component it introduces is the Clinical Decision Support Engine; EMRs, referral tools, e-prescribing and lab systems consume these components.
items.examples: NCD follow-up from community to clinic; antenatal care to delivery; referral and discharge summaries; guideline-based alerts using WHO SMART Guidelines content
items.source: RA 1.5.1; Appendix E (Goal 3); Appendix C (Computable Decision Support Engine)

items.label: Trusted personal health records
items.short_def: Every person has a verifiable digital health record they can see and control, and that authorised providers can trust.
items.long_def: Goal 4 needs each person resolved to a single verifiable identity, a longitudinal record reachable wherever care is given, consent that can be granted, recorded and withdrawn, and assurance that records are authentic. The RA notes this goal introduces no new DPI-H component: it is what the shared data layer exists to serve, through the Client Registry and Lifelong Health Record, backed by trust services and consent. Patient portals and apps consume this foundation rather than being part of DPI-H.
items.examples: Patient portal; digital vaccination record; verifiable health certificate; Australia My Health Record; India ABHA-linked personal health record apps
items.source: RA 1.5.1; Appendix E (Goal 4); RA 2.3 (Principles VIII and IX)

items.label: Climate & epidemic resilience
items.short_def: Detect epidemic and climate-related health threats early enough to act, and coordinate the response.
items.long_def: Goal 7 covers case, syndromic and event-based surveillance and adverse-event reporting, linked to verified people, providers and places so that cases can be confirmed, de-duplicated and located. Its distinctive DPI-H component is the Public Health Surveillance Platform, drawing on the core registries, Terminology Service, Product Registry and HMIS. Uniquely among the goals, its climate dimension relies on weather, climate and environment data from outside the health sector, reached through the same interoperability as the rest of the architecture.
items.examples: Early warning for dengue or measles; climate-sensitive disease reporting; cross-border outbreak information sharing under the IHR; heat-health alerts
items.source: RA 1.5.1; Appendix E (Goal 7); Appendix C (Public Health Surveillance Platform)

items.label: Other: your own use case
items.short_def: A priority use case the team chooses that is not one of the listed options.
items.long_def: Use this when the team's real priority is not IPS or one of the listed goals. The RA advises anchoring early work on two to three high-value goals and specific use cases that have political support and can show value quickly, so describe the use case concretely: who is served, what happens, and what outcome changes. Two RA goals are not listed separately here and fit this option: Goal 5 (supply chain) and Goal 6 (health financing).
items.examples: Supply chain visibility for essential medicines (RA Goal 5); health insurance claims and provider payment (RA Goal 6); NCD registry; birth notification shared with civil registration
items.source: RA 4.1.2; RA 4.2.2 (Phase 1); Appendix E (Goals 5 and 6); Workshop guidance

items.label: National digital health strategy
items.short_def: A government strategy that sets the direction and priorities for digital health.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Current, formally endorsed, and names interoperability as a priority. An endorsed strategy gives partners one direction to align to and is the first step in the RA's roadmap; one that leaves out interoperability tends to produce more disconnected systems.

items.label: National architecture / blueprint
items.short_def: A national map of the shared components, how they connect, and the target state, ideally aligned to the DPI-H RA.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Formally adopted, and partners map their work to it (e.g. OpenHIE in the Philippines). A blueprint only shapes investment when it is adopted and used: new projects should show which components they reuse or provide.
items.examples: Philippines (OpenHIE-based architecture); World Bank Digital Health Blueprint Toolkit

items.label: Costed plan with a budget line
items.short_def: A prioritised, costed plan for digital health, backed by recurrent government funding.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Costed plan, plus a named budget line agreed with the Ministry of Finance. Shared infrastructure must be run and maintained for years; without a recurrent budget line it depends on project funding and tends to stop when projects end.

items.label: Steering body
items.short_def: A senior group that makes digital health decisions across programmes and partners.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Set up by ministerial instrument, has decision authority, and meets on schedule. Without a formal mandate and regular meetings, decisions drift to individual projects and donors.

items.label: Technical Working Group (TWG)
items.short_def: The operational group that reviews standards, systems and partner proposals.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Approves key decisions on a fixed review cycle using a written decision rule. Clinicians hold voting seats. A TWG with a written decision rule makes technical choices predictable for partners; clinical voting seats keep standards tied to how care is actually delivered.

items.label: Named authority for architecture & standards
items.short_def: A named unit or person with the authority to approve standards and check new systems against the architecture.
items.long_def: **Done means:** A person or unit with the power to reject or escalate non-conforming systems. Standards only hold if someone can say no: this is what turns the architecture from guidance into practice.

items.label: National interoperability framework
items.short_def: The agreed rules for how health systems exchange data: standards, identifiers, code sets and exchange patterns.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Agreed standards, identifiers, code sets and exchange patterns (e.g. FHIR, IPS). Gives every implementer the same rulebook, so systems can connect without one-off custom integrations.
items.examples: HL7 FHIR; International Patient Summary (IPS)

items.label: National core data set
items.short_def: The minimum clinical data the country agrees every relevant system should capture the same way.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Clinical data set defined and endorsed through governance. A shared core data set is what makes records comparable and exchangeable; national or regional data sets can be adopted rather than built from scratch.
items.examples: Pacific Core Data for Interoperability (Pacific CDI); Australian Core Data for Interoperability (AU CDI)

items.label: National Release Centre operating
items.short_def: An in-country function that manages clinical terminology (such as SNOMED CT): licensing, quality and change.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Someone in-country handles licensing, quality assurance and change control. A purchased licence alone doesn't count. Terminology needs ongoing care: local extensions, updates and support for implementers. SNOMED CT is free in member countries; SNOMED GPS is a free subset.
items.examples: SNOMED CT National Release Centre; SNOMED GPS

items.label: Health data protection & consent
items.short_def: Law that governs how health data is collected, shared, protected and consented to.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Law in force that covers health data, with defined rules for consent and data sharing. Clear legal rules let systems share data with confidence; without them, exchange either stalls or happens without safeguards.

items.label: Procurement requires open standards
items.short_def: Purchasing rules that require open standards and avoid lock-in to one vendor.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Tenders require open standards/APIs and protect the ability to replace or migrate systems. Procurement is one of the strongest levers a ministry has: it decides whether every new system adds to the shared infrastructure or works around it.

items.label: Client Registry
items.short_def: The health system's trusted list of the people it serves, so each person is recognised as the same person everywhere.
items.long_def: The Client Registry is the national authoritative source of health-specific person identity. It holds the minimum demographics needed to identify someone, issues health identifiers, links the different local identifiers for the same person, and resolves duplicates through matching. It is not a clinical record. It links to national ID or civil registration where these exist but also covers people without legal ID (newborns, refugees, undocumented migrants), making it an equity tool. It underpins the Lifelong Health Record and is reused by surveillance, financing and supply chain functions; it is also called a master patient index (MPI/EMPI).
items.examples: India ABDM (ABHA health ID); Australia Healthcare Identifiers Service (IHI); Open Client Registry (OpenCR); hospital MPI; IHE PIX / PMIR profiles
items.source: RA 1.2.1 (Box 1.2); RA 2.1.1; RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 3.5.3.1; Appendix C (Client Registry); Appendix D.1

items.label: Health Facility Registry
items.short_def: One trusted list of every place where health services are delivered, with its location and type.
items.long_def: The Health Facility Registry is the national authoritative source of identity, location and classification for all health service delivery points, including hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, laboratories, warehouses, outreach sites and temporary posts, across public, private, faith-based and NGO sectors. The registry is the system; the Master Facility List (MFL) is the data it produces. It relies on a cross-sectoral Common Geo-Registry for geography, including how administrative boundaries change over time. With the Health Workforce Registry it shows where and by whom care was given, and it is reused by supply chain, financing and surveillance.
items.examples: India ABDM Health Facility Registry; Australia National Health Services Directory; DHIS2 org-unit lists; Master Facility Lists; IHE mCSD profile
items.source: RA 2.1.1; RA 2.2.1; RA 3.5.3.1; Appendix C (Health Facility Registry)

items.label: Health Workforce Registry
items.short_def: The trusted record of who health workers are, what they are qualified and licensed to do, and where they work.
items.long_def: The Health Workforce Registry is the national authoritative record of identity, credentials and classification for health workers in public and private sectors, including community health workers where nationally registered. It combines identity (who the worker is) with credentials (registration, licensing and qualifications) and links workers to facilities. It is distinct from HR, payroll and learning systems, which use it as their reference. It supports verifying providers at the point of care, preventing payroll and claims fraud, and workforce planning, including data for WHO National Health Workforce Accounts indicators.
items.examples: India ABDM Healthcare Professionals Registry; Australia HPI-I; nursing and medical council databases; IHE mCSD profile
items.source: RA 2.1.1; RA 3.5.3.1; RA 4.3.4; Appendix C (Health Workforce Registry); Appendix E (Goal 2)

items.label: Product Registry
items.short_def: One trusted list of the medicines, vaccines, devices and other health products used in the country.
items.long_def: The Product Registry is the national authoritative source of core identity and classification for medicines, vaccines, medical devices, diagnostics and health commodities. It holds the stable minimum attributes needed to identify a product across sectors, while richer operational detail such as pricing and substitution rules sits in a separate product catalogue tool built on it. It anchors batch and serial traceability, depends on the Terminology Service for classification codes, and with the Facility and Supplier registries forms the master data for the supply chain. The RA frames it as an ongoing master data management programme rather than a one-off system.
items.examples: National essential medicines list; GS1-coded product master (GTIN, GS1 DataMatrix); UDI; national IDMP implementations; GDSN; WHODrug; mSupply product lists
items.source: RA 2.1.1; RA 3.5.3.1; Appendix C (Product Registry); Appendix E (Goal 5)

items.label: Lifelong Health Record
items.short_def: A person's health history over their lifetime, available to them and authorised providers wherever they seek care.
items.long_def: The Lifelong Health Record is the governed, person-centred capability that keeps a longitudinal record of a person's health and care across providers, programmes and time, accessible according to consent and law. It is defined by outcome, not design: a central store, a federated model where data stays at source, or a hybrid are all valid. It is a curated view of clinically relevant data rather than a data lake of everything, and it is part of the minimum foundation alongside the core registries, which tell it who the person is and where and by whom each entry was made. The RA prefers this term to OpenHIE's Shared Health Record.
items.examples: Australia My Health Record; Estonia national health information system; Denmark sundhed.dk; Spain Historia Clínica Digital del SNS; Catalonia HC3; India ABDM federated exchange; Indonesia SATUSEHAT; Philippines Aklan local HIE; HAPI FHIR; EHRbase
items.source: RA 2.2.1; RA 3.5.3.1; Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record); Appendix D.1-D.2

items.label: Terminology Service
items.short_def: A shared service that makes coded health data mean the same thing in every system.
items.long_def: The Terminology Service is a governed, publicly accessible service that manages and publishes code systems, value sets and concept maps, covering international standards and national or local codes. Systems call it to validate codes, fill drop-down lists, look up concepts and translate between code systems. The national service is also the authoritative source for what codes mean, managing how terminologies are adopted, extended and changed. Almost every component depends on it, and it works hand in hand with the Logical Information Model Repository: the TS governs meaning, the LIMR governs structure.
items.examples: SNOMED CT (and SNOMED GPS); ICD-11; LOINC; ATC; ICPC; ICF; Australia NCTS / Ontoserver; Snowstorm; tx.fhir.org; England national terminology service
items.source: RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 3.5.3.1 (Table 3.5); RA 3.6.2; Appendix C (Terminology Service); Appendix D.1

items.label: Logical Information Model Repository
items.short_def: The agreed national blueprints for what each type of health record contains and how it is structured.
items.long_def: The Logical Information Model Repository is a governed repository for technology-independent information models: which data elements a record holds, which are mandatory, their data types and which Terminology Service value sets they use. It makes the structural assumptions hidden in each system's design explicit and shared, so systems do not each structure the same concept differently. FHIR profiles and openEHR archetypes are representations derived from these models, and the LIMR can also hold computable SMART Guidelines content used by the decision support engine. The RA treats it as a progressive enabler that becomes more important as the ecosystem matures, not a prerequisite for the minimum foundation.
items.examples: National FHIR implementation guides and profile registries (e.g. AU Base); openEHR Clinical Knowledge Manager; Spain SOMSNS; WHO SMART Guidelines data dictionaries; Pacific CDI (openEHR models)
items.source: RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 3.5.3.1 (Table 3.5); RA 3.6.2; RA 4.3.1; Appendix C (Logical Information Model Repository); Appendix D

items.label: Computable Decision Support Engine
items.short_def: A shared service that turns guidelines into computer logic and gives recommendations and alerts inside the systems health workers use.
items.long_def: The Computable Decision Support Engine applies computable rules, such as WHO SMART Guidelines and national pathways, to a person's data from the Lifelong Health Record to produce recommendations, alerts, reminders and risk assessments. Its defining feature is that decision logic is kept separate from the applications that use it: rules are governed centrally (via the LIMR) and point-of-care systems call the engine through standard interfaces, so guidance can be updated once for everyone. Its scope can extend beyond clinical care to supply chain, surveillance and financing decisions. Because it needs good data quality and knowledge engineering, the RA treats it as a progressive capability rather than a first step.
items.examples: WHO SMART Guidelines L3 content (antenatal care, HIV, immunisation; pilots in Ethiopia, the Philippines, Uganda); CDS Hooks; CQL / FHIR Clinical Reasoning; OpenCDS; US CDC immunisation logic (CDSi); England national medicines decision support
items.source: RA 2.1.2; RA 3.5.3.2; Appendix C (Computable Decision Support Engine); Appendix D.1-D.3

items.label: Health Management Information System
items.short_def: The shared system that turns routine health data into indicators, dashboards and reports for planning and management.
items.long_def: The Health Management Information System (also called a routine health information system) collects, aggregates and analyses facility- and population-level data for monitoring, programme performance, planning and resource allocation. In DPI-H its defining feature is that it derives indicators from data already captured at the point of care and held in shared infrastructure, reducing parallel reporting burden. It depends on the Lifelong Health Record, the core registries and the Terminology Service, and analytics are treated as part of the HMIS rather than a separate component. It answers population-level questions, complementing the decision support engine, which works at the level of the individual.
items.examples: DHIS2; national HMIS in Tanzania, Uganda and Rwanda; India national HMIS; Spain federated national health information system
items.source: RA 2.1.2; RA 3.5.3.2; Appendix C (Health Management Information System); Appendix D.1-D.2

items.label: Public Health Surveillance Platform
items.short_def: A shared platform that spots disease outbreaks and other health threats early and supports a coordinated response.
items.long_def: The Public Health Surveillance Platform supports case-based, event-based and indicator-based surveillance for early warning, outbreak detection, investigation and response at local, national and international level. It draws on the Client Registry, Health Facility Registry, Terminology Service and Lifelong Health Record so that surveillance data is consistent with clinical data and not collected in parallel. It is distinct from, but exchanges data with, the HMIS, and supports reporting obligations under the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005). It is the distinctive component for the goal of climate and epidemic resilience.
items.examples: DHIS2 Tracker; Go.Data; SORMAS; India Integrated Health Information Platform; US BioSense syndromic surveillance; European Surveillance System (TESSy); Pacific Syndromic Surveillance System
items.source: RA 2.1.2; RA 3.5.3.2; Appendix C (Public Health Surveillance Platform); Appendix D; Appendix E (Goal 7)

items.label: Benefits Package Registry
items.short_def: The official record of what each health coverage scheme covers, for whom, by whom and under what conditions.
items.long_def: The Benefits Package Registry is the national authoritative, machine-readable record of all health benefit packages, including government entitlements, social health insurance, donor, community, private and NGO schemes. It holds definitions, not transactions: it does not enrol people, process claims or manage contracts, which are functions of operational systems that use it as their reference. It draws on the Client, Health Facility and Product registries, and the RA notes it is distinct from the Beneficiary Registry (who is enrolled) and the Contract and Benefits Management System. It was the one genuinely new component identified by the health financing analysis.
items.examples: Social health insurance benefit schedules; government-funded entitlements; donor-supported or disease-specific subsidy schemes
items.source: RA 1.2.3 (Box 1.4); RA 2.4.2; RA 3.5.1; RA 3.5.3.2; Appendix C (Benefits Package Registry)

items.label: Supplier Registry
items.short_def: One trusted list of the organisations that make, import and distribute health products, and whether they are authorised.
items.long_def: The Supplier Registry is the authoritative master data source for the identity, classification and regulatory status of manufacturers, distributors, importers, logistics providers and other supply partners. It holds identity data only; contracts, prices and performance belong to a separate Supplier and Contracts Management System. Together with the Product Registry and Health Facility Registry it forms the master data on which supply chain transactions depend. The RA notes that supplier registries are often owned by finance, procurement, trade or regulatory authorities rather than health, so an existing cross-sectoral registry should be reused where one exists.
items.examples: Regulatory authority supplier lists; procurement vendor masters; GS1 Global Location Numbers (GLN) for supplier locations
items.source: RA 2.1.2; RA 3.5.3.2; Appendix C (Supplier Registry); Appendix E (Goal 5)

items.label: National digital ID
items.short_def: The government-wide system that proves a person's legal identity, which health can link to but does not replace.
items.long_def: Foundational identity (national ID, population register) is owned outside the health sector and is the authoritative source of a person's legal identity. The RA shows why it is necessary but not sufficient for health: it may not cover newborns, refugees or undocumented migrants, does not show eligibility or consent, and cannot do clinical matching. The Client Registry therefore links to national ID where possible (for example by validating identity through an API) and works without it where it is absent or inaccessible.
items.examples: National ID systems (e.g. India Aadhaar); Estonia national digital identity; population registers
items.source: RA 1.2.1 (Box 1.2); RA 2.1.3; RA 4.3.4; Appendix C (Client Registry)

items.label: Trust services
items.short_def: Shared digital certificates and signatures that let systems and countries check documents are genuine and unaltered.
items.long_def: Trust services include public key infrastructure (PKI), certificate authorities, digital signatures and verifiable credentials. The RA treats these as foundational DPI that health should build on rather than duplicate, used for authenticating users and providers and proving where data came from. Across borders, WHO's Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) lets authorities verify each other's health documents without centralising personal data.
items.examples: National PKI and certificate authorities; digital signatures; verifiable credentials; WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN)
items.source: RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 2.3 (Principle IX); RA 3.6.4; Appendix C (Client Registry)

items.label: Payments
items.short_def: Government-wide payment rails that move money once health systems have decided who should be paid and how much.
items.long_def: Foundational payments DPI, such as instant payment systems, mobile money and government-to-person transfers, moves and settles funds securely at scale. The RA notes it cannot make health-specific decisions such as eligibility, claim adjudication or provider verification; those are made by health financing systems using the Benefits Package Registry and other registries. Payments DPI then executes provider and workforce payments and collection of contributions.
items.examples: Instant payment systems (e.g. Brazil Pix); mobile money; government-to-person (G2P) transfers; payment gateway APIs

items.label: Government data exchange
items.short_def: Government-wide secure data pipes that carry data between authorised systems without reading it.
items.long_def: Foundational data exchange provides secure, authenticated, logged transport between registered systems, with signed and time-stamped logs and data-sharing agreements. The RA compares it to a postal service that delivers sealed envelopes: it should not interpret or transform clinical content, which stays the job of health systems and health standards. Where it is mature, health should reuse it; where it is absent, health may need interim exchange capability designed to align with it later.
items.examples: Estonia X-Road; GovStack Information Mediator; whole-of-government data exchange platforms

items.label: Civil registration (CRVS)
items.short_def: The national system that officially records births, deaths and their causes.
items.long_def: Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) is foundational, cross-sector infrastructure owned outside the health sector. The RA expects birth and death events to update the Client Registry and Health Workforce Registry, and gives the example of a facility publishing a birth once for both civil registration and the immunisation registry. Cause-of-death recording uses ICD.
items.examples: National civil registration systems; birth and death notification from facilities
items.source: RA 3.5.1; RA 3.6.3; RA 4.3.4; Appendix C (Client Registry)

items.label: Geo-registry & notifications
items.short_def: Shared government maps and boundaries, messaging channels, and weather and climate data that health systems can reuse.
items.long_def: A Common Geo-Registry is a cross-sector foundational registry of administrative units, settlements and boundaries, including how they change over time; the Health Facility Registry relies on it rather than reproducing it. The RA also points to a foundational weather, climate and environment data capability, outside health, used for the climate and epidemic resilience goal. Shared notification channels (SMS, email, push) let health services send alerts and reminders.
items.examples: Common Geo-Registry (GeoLab guidance); national geo-registries; SMS gateways; national meteorological and climate data services
items.source: RA 3.5.1; Appendix C (Health Facility Registry); Appendix E (Goal 7); RA Integrated View

items.label: Information mediator (HIE / API gateway)
items.short_def: The function that connects health systems so they can exchange data securely, whether through a central hub or distributed connections.
items.long_def: The information mediator routes messages, authenticates parties, orchestrates multi-step transactions and logs exchanges for audit. The RA stresses that mediation is a role, not a single box to buy: it can be delivered through a central service bus, distributed access points, gateways in front of components, direct standards-based connections, or a mix, and the RA does not prescribe one. Whatever the pattern, exchange should follow open specifications, authenticate and audit participants, and avoid unmanaged point-to-point links. Where government-wide data exchange exists, health should reuse it for transport and add only the health-specific content standards.
items.examples: REST APIs (FHIR R4); event streams (subscriptions / publish-subscribe); document exchange (IHE); federated query; bulk data ($export); cross-border exchange (IHR / IPS); national HIEs (e.g. Kenya, Rwanda); OpenHIM; Philippines Aklan local HIE
items.source: RA 3.6 intro; RA 3.6.1; RA 3.6.3 (Figure 3.6); RA 4.3.4; RA 5.2; RA Integrated View

items.label: Consent service
items.short_def: A shared way to record a person's consent decisions and make sure systems act on them when health data is shared.
items.long_def: The RA lists consent, authorisation and privacy among the REDDHI foundational capabilities, delivered either by a health-sector consent service with consent enforced where data is exchanged, or by national cross-sector consent infrastructure where it exists. Consent should be represented in a common, standards-based form that travels with the data; enforcement rests with the systems holding and exchanging the data and with national law. The RA deliberately does not set the rules on what counts as valid consent or who may give it, which are matters for each country. Because cross-sector consent infrastructure is still uncommon, a health-specific service may be needed, designed to connect to national infrastructure later.
items.examples: HL7 FHIR Consent resource; IHE privacy and consent profiles; Australia My Health Record access controls; India ABDM consent manager
items.source: RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 2.3 (Principle VIII); RA 1.2.1 (Box 1.2, item 3); RA 3.6.3

items.label: National digital ID
items.short_def: The government-wide system that establishes and verifies who a person is, and whether health services are allowed to use it.
items.long_def: National digital ID is foundational DPI that health should build on where it exists, is trusted and is legally usable for health. The RA stresses that it is necessary but not sufficient: it often misses newborns, refugees, undocumented migrants and others the health sector must serve, and it does not cover eligibility, consent or clinical matching. The Client Registry therefore links to national ID where possible while still covering people without it. When rating this enabler, consider coverage, legal permission for health use, and whether a technical integration route exists.
items.examples: India Aadhaar; Philippines PhilSys; Estonia ID-card and Mobile-ID; civil registration numbers issued at birth

items.label: Consent & privacy
items.short_def: The laws, rules and services that let people give, refuse and withdraw consent for their health data to be shared.
items.long_def: This enabler covers both the legal rules on consent and any shared service that records and applies consent decisions across sectors. The RA expects health data to need finer-grained consent than general identity systems provide, for example sharing with a doctor but not with researchers. Where a country has cross-sector consent infrastructure, health should consider building on it; where it does not, a health-sector consent capability may be needed that can align with national infrastructure later.
items.examples: National data protection act consent provisions; India DEPA consent managers; HL7 FHIR Consent; opt-out arrangements for national health record systems

items.label: Data exchange / interoperability layer
items.short_def: The shared means by which systems securely send and receive data, such as a government data exchange or a health information exchange.
items.long_def: Foundational data exchange provides secure, authenticated and logged transport between registered systems, but, like a postal service, it does not read the content. The RA says health should reuse government exchange where it is mature and add only the health-specific content, terminology and consent rules at the endpoints; where none exists, health may run its own exchange in the interim, designed to align later. The RA does not prescribe a pattern: distributed access points, a service bus, gateways or direct standards-based links can coexist.
items.examples: Estonia X-Road; GovStack Information Mediator building block; national HIEs (e.g. Kenya, Rwanda); OpenHIM

items.label: Trust & digital signatures (e.g. WHO GDHCN)
items.short_def: Public key infrastructure, digital signatures and trust networks that let organisations confirm a document or system is genuine.
items.long_def: Trust services let participants verify who they are dealing with and that data has not been altered. The RA asks countries to build on national trust infrastructure (PKI, certificate authorities, digital signature or verifiable credential services) where it exists, and allows graduated assurance, starting with simpler checks where it does not. For cross-border use, WHO's Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) lets participating authorities verify each other's signed health documents without centralising personal data.
items.examples: National PKI and certificate authorities; WHO GDHCN; digitally signed vaccination certificates (e.g. ICVP); verifiable credentials for health worker licences

items.label: Payments
items.short_def: Government-wide payment rails used to pay providers and health workers and to collect contributions.
items.long_def: Foundational payments DPI, such as instant payment systems, mobile money and government-to-person transfers, moves money securely and at scale. The RA notes it executes payments only after health-specific decisions have been made, such as claim adjudication, eligibility and confirming that the payee is licensed; those decisions belong to health financing components such as the Benefits Package Registry. Rate this enabler by whether health payments can actually run over the national rails today.
items.examples: India UPI; mobile money (e.g. M-Pesa); government-to-person transfer systems; treasury payment systems for payroll

items.label: Governance / legal framework
items.short_def: The laws, policies and governance bodies that authorise, fund and oversee digital health and shared health data.
items.long_def: The RA treats legislation as one of five sustainability dimensions: the right to operate shared infrastructure, share data across programmes and require conformance all rest on it. A national assessment should check whether a legal framework for health data exists, whether there is a designated home for architecture decisions, and whether procurement supports open standards. Governance structures differ by country; the RA describes principles and leaves specific bodies to national legal and institutional context.
items.examples: Digital health strategy or eHealth policy; data protection law covering health data; health information or eHealth act; national digital health steering committee

items.label: Provider systems
items.short_def: Systems that health facilities and clinicians use day to day, such as electronic medical records, hospital and laboratory systems.
items.long_def: These point-of-care and functional applications record and act on care: electronic medical and health records, hospital information systems, laboratory and imaging systems, e-prescribing and telemedicine. The RA places them outside DPI-H: they use the shared infrastructure (client, facility and workforce registries, Terminology Service, Lifelong Health Record, decision support engine) rather than form part of it. DPI-H defines what these systems need so they can be built, connected and run well, without prescribing which products a country buys.
items.examples: EMR/EHR/HIS; LIMS, PACS and RIS; e-prescribing; telemedicine clients
items.source: RA 2.1; RA 3.5.1; Appendix E (Goal 3); RA Integrated View

items.label: Case management
items.short_def: Programme systems that track individual people through care, such as immunisation, HIV, TB, and maternal and child health registers.
items.long_def: Case management systems support disease-specific and programme workflows, including registration into a programme, follow-up and reporting. In the RA these are functional applications that consume DPI-H, for example using the Client Registry to identify people and the Terminology Service for coding, rather than keeping their own parallel person and facility lists. The RA gives the example of a facility publishing a birth event once so that both the civil registration system and the electronic immunisation registry can act on it.
items.examples: Electronic immunisation registry; HIV/TB/MNCH registries; disease-specific tools; follow-up workflows
items.source: RA 2.1; RA 3.5.1; RA 3.6.3; Appendix E (Goals 3 and 7); RA Integrated View

items.label: Pharmacy & dispensing
items.short_def: Systems for managing pharmacies, dispensing medicines and reporting medicine safety problems.
items.long_def: Pharmacy applications handle dispensing, stock at the point of service and pharmacovigilance (adverse-event reporting). The RA classes dispensing and adverse-event applications as operational systems outside DPI-H. They rely on the Product Registry for consistent product identity, the Client Registry where dispensing is traced to an individual, and the Benefits Package Registry for coverage rules.
items.examples: Pharmacy management systems; dispensing apps; pharmacovigilance and adverse-event reporting; inventory at point of service
items.source: RA 2.1; Appendix E (Goals 5 and 7); RA Integrated View

items.label: CHW & community
items.short_def: Tools used by community health workers and outreach teams, often designed to work without a constant internet connection.
items.long_def: Community health worker (CHW) applications support household registration, outreach visits and community-level data collection. They sit outside DPI-H but draw on it: the Health Workforce Registry can include nationally recognised CHW cadres, and community programme data can flow into the Lifelong Health Record and the HMIS. The RA notes that store-and-forward exchange allows such tools to keep working when connectivity is intermittent and to sync later.
items.examples: CHW field apps; outreach tools; offline-first tooling; household registration
items.source: RA 2.1; RA 3.6.3; Appendix C (Health Workforce Registry, Lifelong Health Record); RA Integrated View

items.label: Citizen / patient apps
items.short_def: Apps that people use themselves to see their health information, book services and manage who can see their data.
items.long_def: Citizen-facing apps include personal health records or digital health wallets, self-service booking, alerts and consent dashboards. The RA states that patient-facing applications use the shared foundation, mainly the Client Registry, Lifelong Health Record and consent capability, rather than being defined by DPI-H. They give practical effect to people's right to access and control their health information.
items.examples: Personal health record / digital health wallet; self-service booking; citizen alerting; consent dashboard
items.source: RA 2.3 (Principle VIII); Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record); Appendix E (Goal 4); RA Integrated View

items.label: Supply chain
items.short_def: Operational systems that move health products from supplier to patient: forecasting, ordering, warehousing, transport and cold chain.
items.long_def: Supply chain applications cover forecasting, procurement, warehouse and logistics management, transport and cold-chain monitoring, including tracking batches and serial numbers. The RA puts these outside DPI-H: they consume three shared reference registries, Product, Health Facility (locations) and Supplier, which the RA calls the master data pillars of all supply chain transactions. Richer operational tools such as a product catalogue or supplier and contracts management system build on these registries rather than replacing them.
items.examples: WMS/LMIS; transport management (TMS); procurement / e-tender; cold-chain monitoring
items.source: RA 2.1; Appendix C (Product Registry, Supplier Registry); Appendix E (Goal 5); RA Integrated View

items.label: Coverage & claims
items.short_def: Systems that enrol members of health coverage schemes, process claims and manage contracts with providers.
items.long_def: Coverage and claims applications include claims authoring and adjudication, beneficiary (member) registries, member and provider portals, and contract and benefit management. The RA places these in the functional application layer: they consume the Benefits Package Registry (what is covered and under what conditions), the Client Registry, and the facility and workforce registries for provider accreditation. Payment itself is executed by foundational payments DPI once these systems have made their decisions.
items.examples: Claims authoring and adjudication; beneficiary registry; member and provider portals; contract and benefits management systems; claims exchange
items.source: RA 1.2.3; RA 2.4.2; RA 3.5.1; Appendix C (Benefits Package Registry); RA 4.3.4; RA Integrated View

items.label: Finance & workforce ops
items.short_def: Government finance, budgeting, payroll, human resources and training systems used to run the health system.
items.long_def: These include public financial management systems (IFMIS/treasury), health budget planning, human resources information systems (HRIS), payroll and learning management systems (LMS), plus audit and disclosure tools. The RA treats them as operational systems outside DPI-H. HRIS and LMS use the Health Workforce Registry as their reference source for who a health worker is and what they may do, and payroll can be checked against it to detect inactive or unqualified staff.
items.examples: IFMIS / treasury; HFIS / budget planning; HRIS, payroll and LMS; audit and disclosure tools
items.source: RA 1.2.3; RA 2.4.2; Appendix C (Health Workforce Registry); Appendix E (Goal 2); RA Integrated View

items.label: Public health apps
items.short_def: Tools for managing outbreaks, tracing contacts, viewing surveillance data and sending alerts.
items.long_def: Public health applications support case reporting, outbreak management, contact tracing, surveillance dashboards and alerting of health workers. The RA describes these as operational systems that consume DPI-H, especially the Public Health Surveillance Platform, the registries for linking cases to verified people, providers and places, and the HMIS, rather than as DPI-H components. Several such tools are named in the RA only as illustrations of how the surveillance capability has been delivered.
items.examples: Contact tracing; outbreak management; surveillance dashboards; outbreak alerting (RA illustrative tools: Go.Data, SORMAS, DHIS2 Tracker)
items.source: Appendix D.1 (Public Health Surveillance Platform); Appendix E (Goal 7); RA Integrated View

items.label: HL7 FHIR
items.short_def: The main international standard for exchanging health data between systems over the web, in small reusable building blocks called resources.
items.long_def: HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) defines standard data resources and web APIs for health data. The RA recommends it as the framework for specifying and implementing DPI-H exchange services, with FHIR profiles defining the resources, operations and searches each component supports. It provides the structural layer of interoperability, but the RA cautions that two systems can both be valid FHIR and still differ in meaning unless they follow the same governed information model and terminology. Countries can start with simpler exchange and move towards FHIR, provided their data models are aligned from the outset.
items.examples: National FHIR implementation guides; FHIR profiles for each registry; FHIR terminology operations ($expand, $validate-code, $translate); HAPI FHIR; Firely Server

items.label: IPS
items.short_def: International Patient Summary: an agreed minimum set of key health information that can travel with a person across borders.
items.long_def: The IPS is an HL7 FHIR standard for a short patient summary, covering for example allergies, current medicines and significant history. The RA names it as the shared, internationally aligned specification that should define the meaningful minimum for cross-border care, used together with terminology translation, a cross-jurisdiction trust framework and explicit legal and consent arrangements. It is also a content specification that can shape national exchange.
items.examples: HL7 FHIR IPS implementation guide; European cross-border patient summary exchange

items.label: IHE
items.short_def: Integrating the Healthcare Enterprise: ready-made specifications for common exchange tasks, such as patient lookup, directories and document sharing.
items.long_def: IHE publishes integration profiles that define the actors and transactions for common health exchange scenarios, building on standards such as HL7 and DICOM. The RA can adopt IHE specifications directly: where an exchange matches an IHE transaction, it names the actor and transaction and relies on the IHE specification and IHE conformance testing for the detail. Appendix C references IHE profiles for the client, facility and workforce registries and for consent.
items.examples: PIX and PMIR (patient identity); mCSD (facility and health worker directory); SVCM (terminology); IHE privacy and consent profiles; IHE document sharing; IHE Connectathons
items.source: RA 3.6.2; RA 3.7.3; RA 2.3 (Principle VIII); Appendix C (Client Registry, Health Facility Registry, Health Workforce Registry, Terminology Service)

items.label: openEHR
items.short_def: An open standard for defining clinical data as shared, reusable models that clinicians help design.
items.long_def: openEHR uses archetypes and templates to define clinical content (for example a blood pressure reading) independently of any software. The RA lists openEHR alongside FHIR as a way to express and publish the logical information models held in the LIMR, and as a basis for clinical data repositories and archetype-based decision support. It illustrates the RA's point that aligning information models helps interoperability whichever technology is used.
items.examples: openEHR Clinical Knowledge Manager (CKM); EHRbase; GDL2 decision support; Pacific CDI
items.source: RA 3.5.3.1 (Table 3.5); Appendix C (Logical Information Model Repository); Appendix D.1

items.label: SNOMED CT
items.short_def: A detailed clinical terminology for recording diagnoses, findings, procedures and other clinical facts in a consistent, codable way.
items.long_def: SNOMED CT is one of the clinical terminologies the RA references for giving data consistent meaning across systems. It is hosted and governed through the Terminology Service, often with national extensions managed by a national release centre. The RA notes that SNOMED CT requires a licence (free in member countries of SNOMED International), while SNOMED GPS is a freely available subset suitable for implementation and evaluation.
items.examples: SNOMED CT International Edition; SNOMED GPS; national editions (e.g. SNOMED CT UK Edition)
items.source: RA 2.2.2 (incl. footnote); RA 3.4.5; RA 3.6.2; Appendix C (Terminology Service)

items.label: ICD-10 / 11
items.short_def: WHO's International Classification of Diseases, used to classify diseases and causes of death for statistics and reporting.
items.long_def: ICD is the WHO classification used for morbidity and mortality statistics, reporting and often for financing and coding of services. The RA lists ICD (including ICD-11) among the established classifications that give data consistent meaning across systems and borders, hosted through the Terminology Service and mapped to clinical terminologies where needed.
items.examples: ICD-10; ICD-11

items.label: LOINC
items.short_def: Standard codes for laboratory tests and clinical measurements, so results mean the same thing everywhere.
items.long_def: LOINC provides codes for laboratory and clinical observations. The RA lists it among the core terminologies managed through the Terminology Service, and uses it to illustrate concept maps, for example linking a LOINC code and a SNOMED CT concept for systolic blood pressure.
items.examples: LOINC laboratory and observation codes (e.g. 8480-6 systolic blood pressure)
items.source: RA 2.2.2; RA 3.5.3.1 (Table 3.5); RA 3.6.2; Appendix C (Terminology Service)

items.label: GS1
items.short_def: Global barcode and identification standards for products and locations, such as GTIN for products and GLN for places.
items.long_def: GS1 standards give products, batches and locations globally unique identifiers that can be carried in barcodes. The RA references GS1 for product identification and traceability in the Product Registry and for identifying supplier and facility locations, as part of the master data on which supply chain transactions depend.
items.examples: GTIN; GS1 DataMatrix; GLN; GDSN
items.source: RA 3.6.2; Appendix C (Product Registry, Supplier Registry, Health Facility Registry)

items.label: SMART Guidelines
items.short_def: WHO guidelines turned into reusable digital content, from narrative recommendations to computable decision logic, that countries can adapt.
items.long_def: SMART stands for Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based and Testable. WHO SMART Guidelines package recommendations as digital adaptation kits (data dictionaries, workflows, decision tables) and as computable FHIR content (L3) that a Clinical Decision Support Engine can run. The RA counts them as open content within the full-STAC enabling conditions; they are not a DPI-H component themselves. They are distinct from SMART on FHIR, an app-launch and authorisation standard.
items.examples: Antenatal care, HIV, immunisation and family planning digital adaptation kits; L3 pilots in Ethiopia, the Philippines and Uganda
items.source: RA Glossary; RA 2.2.2; Appendix C (Computable Decision Support Engine); Appendix D.3

items.label: DICOM
items.short_def: The international standard for storing and sharing medical images, such as X-rays and scans.
items.long_def: DICOM defines formats and communication for medical imaging. The RA lists it as the standard it references for imaging; imaging systems themselves are functional applications that use DPI-H rather than part of it.

items.label: Exists
items.short_def: The component exists at national scale, is in routine use and is trusted as the authoritative source.
items.long_def: Choose Exists only when all three hold: it covers the whole country or all the programmes it should, it is used in day-to-day work, and other systems rely on it rather than keeping their own copies. The RA's markers of progress are useful checks: is it authoritative, reused across programmes, exchanged through governed, standards-based means, and is its data quality actively managed? If any of these is clearly missing, Partial is usually the better answer.
items.examples: A national facility registry that HMIS, supply chain and surveillance all read from; a client registry issuing health IDs nationwide

items.label: Partial
items.short_def: Something exists, but only for some sites or programmes, or it is not trusted or reused as the authoritative source.
items.long_def: Partial is the most common answer and covers several situations: a pilot or subnational deployment, a system used by one programme only, several competing versions of the same list, or a national system that others do not rely on because its data is out of date or not standards-based. Use the notes to say which of these applies, because each implies a different next step (scale up, consolidate, upgrade to open standards, or fix governance). The RA's entry points describe these as integrating or upgrading existing systems rather than starting from zero.
items.examples: An immunisation registry with its own patient list; a facility list kept in a spreadsheet by HMIS only; an EMR-based patient index covering a few hospitals
items.source: Workshop guidance (Sydney worksheet); RA 4.1.1; RA 4.2.1 (entry points 2 and 3)

items.label: Absent
items.short_def: Nothing that performs this function is in place yet.
items.long_def: Choose Absent when no system or agreed shared list performs this function, or when the only traces are paper records or a pilot that has ended. Absent is not a failure: for many components it is the normal starting point, and the RA's ground-up entry point recommends setting governance and standards before buying technology. If the function is partly done inside another system, Partial is more accurate.
items.examples: No national health worker register; no terminology service, with codes hard-wired in each application

items.label: Subnational
items.short_def: Best built or run by a province, state or district, within national rules and standards.
items.long_def: Choose Subnational when the function is delivered close to care and differs by area, for example where provinces run their own health services or systems, provided national standards and identifiers are respected so that data can still be combined nationally. The RA leaves central, federated or hybrid implementation as a national choice, as long as each registry has a single accountable authoritative source. Its governance principle of subsidiarity places decisions at the lowest level able to make them well.
items.examples: Provincial EMR or local health information exchange feeding the national record; state-run facility data maintained under a national registry standard; Spain's Catalonia region
items.source: RA 3.4.1; RA 3.4.2 (Subsidiarity); RA 4.2.2 (Phase 3); Appendix D.2 (Spain, Catalonia); Workshop guidance

items.label: National
items.short_def: Best built or agreed once for the whole country.
items.long_def: Choose National when the component must be a single authoritative reference for the country, such as the core registries, the national terminology and the rules for exchange and trust. The RA treats these as shared infrastructure governed in the public interest under national control, even when parts are run by provinces or contractors. National scope does not mean a single central database; it means one accountable owner and one set of rules.
items.examples: National client, facility and health workforce registries; national terminology release; national exchange specifications
items.source: RA 1.4 (Autonomy and Sovereignty); RA 2.1.1; RA 3.4.1; Workshop guidance (Sydney worksheet)

items.label: Regional
items.short_def: Could be built or agreed once, together, across several countries.
items.long_def: Choose Regional when several countries face the same need and one shared artefact or service would cost less or work better than each building its own, such as a regional terminology subset, a shared implementation guide, a trust network or shared training. The RA describes layered governance: a regional body with explicit authority over what is shared, national bodies for what is country-specific, and clear handoff points. Personal health data stays national; cross-border exchange is federated through national gateways.
items.examples: Regional patient summary or vaccination certificate profile; shared SNOMED CT subset or licence arrangement; regional surveillance network; joint capacity-building programme

items.label: Technical assistance
items.short_def: Expert help to design, specify or implement a component or arrangement.
items.long_def: Technical assistance means outside experts working with the team on a defined task, such as an architecture assessment, writing specifications, configuring a registry or reviewing vendor conformance. Choose it when the skills are needed for a specific piece of work; choose Training instead when the aim is lasting in-country skill. The RA cautions against depending indefinitely on external consultants, so assistance works best when it transfers skills.
items.examples: Architecture assessment and roadmap; FHIR profile development; registry deployment support; procurement specification review

items.label: Funding
items.short_def: Money to build a component or to keep it running.
items.long_def: Funding covers both one-off implementation costs and the recurrent costs of operating shared infrastructure. The RA stresses that running costs are often underestimated and that sustained financing, ideally a recurrent domestic budget line, matters as much as the initial build. When choosing this, say whether the gap is capital, recurrent, or both.
items.examples: Grant to deploy a facility registry; co-financing of hosting and support for three years; budget for terminology licences
items.source: RA 3.4.2 (Financial sustainability); RA 4.6.1; RA 4.6.3; Workshop guidance

items.label: Training / capacity
items.short_def: Building the lasting skills of staff to design, run, use and govern the systems.
items.long_def: Training and capacity covers national architects, modellers, terminologists and informaticians as well as front-line users and data managers. The RA calls this a national capability question rather than a series of hires, and notes that change management, workflow redesign and stakeholder engagement need as much planning as the technology. Choose this when the gap is skills that must stay in the country.
items.examples: National digital health leadership programme; FHIR and terminology training for ministry staff; user training for a new registry

items.label: Standards / licensing (e.g. SNOMED)
items.short_def: Access to the standards, terminologies and licences needed to give data a shared structure and meaning.
items.long_def: This covers obtaining and adopting standards such as HL7 FHIR, IPS, ICD-11, LOINC and SNOMED CT, including licences, national release arrangements and guidance on which to use. The RA notes SNOMED CT is free in member countries of SNOMED International and licensed directly elsewhere, while SNOMED GPS is a freely available subset. Choose this when the barrier is access to, or choice of, standards rather than the skills to use them.
items.examples: SNOMED International membership or licence; national ICD-11 adoption; access to WHO SMART Guidelines content; FHIR implementation guides
items.source: RA 2.2.2 (incl. footnote); RA 3.6.2; Appendix C (Terminology Service); Workshop guidance

items.label: Policy / governance
items.short_def: Help with the policy, legal and governance arrangements that give shared infrastructure its mandate.
items.long_def: Policy and governance support helps with laws, regulations, decision rights and governance bodies: for example drafting health data regulations, setting up an architecture governance body, defining who is custodian of which data, or agreeing a cross-border legal basis. The RA states that governance comes before technology and that legislation gives shared infrastructure a durable basis. Choose this when the team knows what it wants to build but lacks the mandate to do it.
items.examples: Drafting a health data or eHealth regulation; terms of reference for a digital health steering committee; data-sharing agreements; consent policy

items.label: Peer learning
items.short_def: Learning directly from other countries that have faced the same problem.
items.long_def: Peer learning includes study visits, communities of practice and regional networks where ministries share plans, artefacts and lessons. The RA highlights regional and global networks of national architects and implementers as a way to compare approaches and avoid starting from scratch. Choose this when another country has already solved a similar problem and its experience would shorten the path.
items.examples: Regional architect network meetings; study visit to a country with a working registry; sharing implementation guides or terminology subsets

items.label: SPC
items.short_def: The Pacific Community: the main intergovernmental scientific and technical organisation serving Pacific island countries and territories.
items.long_def: SPC is owned by its Pacific island member countries and territories together with several founding metropolitan members, and its Public Health Division supports health information, disease surveillance and laboratory networks across the region. Choose it in the workshop when the regional effort is primarily among Pacific island countries and territories.
items.examples: Pacific Public Health Surveillance Network; regional health information and data support to Pacific ministries

items.label: AeHIN
items.short_def: The Asia eHealth Information Network: a regional network of digital health practitioners from ministries and partners across Asia and the Pacific.
items.long_def: AeHIN is a peer network that supports countries through convenings, peer learning and capacity building on digital health governance, architecture, programme management and standards (its Mind the GAPS approach). Choose it in the workshop when the regional effort is mainly about shared learning, capacity and standards across Asian and Pacific countries.
items.examples: AeHIN annual general meetings; regional communities of practice on interoperability and identity

items.label: WHO
items.short_def: The World Health Organization, including its Western Pacific (WPRO) and South-East Asia (SEARO) regional offices.
items.long_def: WHO is the United Nations specialised agency for health. In digital health it sets global norms and guidance (including this Reference Architecture, with ITU), maintains SMART Guidelines and the GDHCN, and provides technical support to ministries through regional and country offices. Choose it in the workshop when the regional effort concerns norms, guidance or trust services that WHO convenes.
items.examples: Global Strategy on Digital Health; WHO SMART Guidelines; Global Digital Health Certification Network; Digital Implementation Investment Guide
items.source: Workshop guidance (Sydney worksheet); RA 2.2.2; RA 3.6.4; RA 4.2.2

items.label: Other
items.short_def: Another organisation the team names as best placed to lead.
items.long_def: Use this when a different body is better placed to lead the regional effort, for example another regional organisation, a development bank, a standards body or a lead country. Name the organisation and say briefly why it fits.
items.examples: A lead country acting for a group; a standards development organisation; a development bank

items.label: Blocks us now
items.short_def: Without it, this use case cannot work today.
items.long_def: Choose this when the gap stops the chosen use case at the first step: for example, there is no way to identify the patient, no legal basis to share the data, or no list of facilities to send it to. A useful test is whether the use case could run even in a basic, manual or limited form without it; if not, it blocks you now. Keep this category short so it points to what must come first.
items.examples: No legal basis to send a patient summary across a border; no client identifier to match records
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas)

items.label: Needed in 12 months
items.short_def: Not blocking today, but needed within the next 12 months.
items.long_def: Choose this when the use case can start, perhaps in a limited or manual way, but will stall or fail to scale within about a year unless the gap is closed. Typical examples are things needed to move from pilot to routine use, such as governance, terminology or conformance testing. These are good candidates for planning and budget requests now.
items.examples: Semantic governance for a growing code list; conformance testing before a second vendor connects
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas); RA 4.2.2

items.label: Can wait
items.short_def: Missing, but not needed for this use case for now.
items.long_def: Choose this when the gap is real but this use case does not depend on it, or only needs it at a later stage of maturity. Recording it is still useful, because another use case may need it sooner. The RA notes that some capabilities, such as the Logical Information Model Repository, can be built up as maturity grows rather than first.
items.examples: Advanced analytics for a use case still at the data-capture stage; a national information model repository while core registries are being set up
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas); RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2)

items.label: Start narrow
items.short_def: Begin with one population, one credential or one facility type, and widen later.
items.long_def: Start narrow limits the first step to a small, well-defined scope so it can work end to end and show value quickly. The RA supports this sequencing: a country focusing on one goal sets up first the components that goal depends on, and extends them as further goals are taken on. The risk to manage is that the narrow start becomes another silo, so build it on shared identifiers and standards from the beginning.
items.examples: Malaysia's Hajj Health Card; digital vaccination certificates for travellers only; a client registry starting with maternal and child health clinics
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas); RA 4.1.2; RA 4.2.2 (Phase 2)

items.label: Start shared
items.short_def: Build the foundation once so that several programmes use it, rather than once for a single use case.
items.long_def: Start shared means investing first in a component several programmes need, such as a client or facility registry, and connecting programmes to it. This is the RA's core reusability principle: shared components avoid duplicated spending and the rapidly growing cost of connecting many separate systems. It usually needs stronger cross-programme governance and pooled funding up front.
items.examples: Thailand's registry used across government; one facility registry serving HMIS, supply chain and surveillance
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas); RA 1.3.1; RA 1.4 (Reusability); RA 4.6.3

items.label: Start borrowed
items.short_def: Adopt a regional or international artefact instead of writing your own.
items.long_def: Start borrowed means reusing an existing specification, guideline, code set or trust arrangement and adapting it locally, rather than designing from scratch. The RA's full-STAC enabling conditions (open standards, technologies, architectures and content) exist so that countries can adapt and build on shared work, and its semantic governance model passes global content down while feeding local needs back up. Check licensing and the governance for local adaptations before adopting.
items.examples: The ICVP implementation guide; the IPS; a SNOMED CT subset (e.g. SNOMED GPS); WHO SMART Guidelines digital adaptation kits
items.source: Workshop guidance (DPI-H for Health Workshop, policy-maker canvas); RA 2.2.2; RA 3.4.5

items.label: Architecture authority
items.short_def: Who decides which building blocks are national, and which systems must connect to them.
items.long_def: This decision covers the national architecture: which components are shared, how they are implemented (central, federated or hybrid), and whether a new system may proceed. The RA recommends a national digital architect function embedded in government with authority to set standards, check conformance and say no or escalate, with major cross-cutting changes approved through strategic governance. In the workshop, name who actually holds this today, which may differ from who should.
items.examples: Ministry of Health digital health unit; national digital health agency; whole-of-government digital authority; digital health steering committee

items.label: Standards mandate
items.short_def: Who decides which standards are required, including as a condition in procurement.
items.long_def: This decision sets the national standards (for example HL7 FHIR, ICD-11, SNOMED CT, LOINC and national profiles) and makes them binding. The RA asks countries to treat architectural conformance as a mandatory procurement requirement and to consider conformance certification as a condition of approval. Without someone holding this mandate, new systems keep adding to legacy debt.
items.examples: National interoperability standards catalogue; ministerial directive mandating FHIR; standards clauses in tender templates

items.label: Core data set custodian
items.short_def: Who maintains the national core data set and the codes it uses, and approves changes to them.
items.long_def: This decision covers stewardship of the agreed national data definitions and code lists, which the RA places in operational governance (master data management) and the Semantic Governance Infrastructure, using the Terminology Service and Logical Information Model Repository. The RA notes custodianship is often split, with different authorities owning different data, for example the medicines regulator for product data. A clear, documented assignment of who owns which data avoids both paralysis and duplicate versions.
items.examples: National health data dictionary owner; national release centre for SNOMED CT; health information standards committee

items.label: Trust anchor
items.short_def: Who signs on behalf of the health sector, and decides whether to accept other countries' signatures.
items.long_def: The trust anchor holds the keys and certificates that make health documents verifiable, and decides which external issuers to trust. The RA advises building on national PKI and signature services where they exist rather than creating a parallel basis for trust, so this role may sit with a whole-of-government authority rather than in health. For cross-border use it links to trust networks such as WHO's GDHCN, which requires an explicit cross-jurisdiction trust framework.
items.examples: National certificate authority; ministry acting as issuer for vaccination certificates; country participant in WHO GDHCN

items.label: Law
items.short_def: The decision right is set in legislation passed by parliament.
items.long_def: Choose Law when an act names who holds this decision. This is the most durable basis: it survives changes of government and funding, and the RA notes that the right to operate shared infrastructure, share data and require conformance rests on legislation. Record the act if known. If a bill is only drafted, choose the basis that applies today.
items.examples: Health information act; digital health agency establishment act; data protection act naming a regulator

items.label: Decree
items.short_def: The decision right is set by a ministerial or executive decree, order or regulation.
items.long_def: Choose Decree when the authority comes from an executive instrument rather than an act of parliament, such as a ministerial order, regulation or circular. It is quicker to create than law but easier to change, and may not bind other ministries or private providers. The RA leaves the specific instruments to each country's legal and institutional context.
items.examples: Ministerial order mandating a national standard; executive order creating a steering committee; regulation under a public health act

items.label: TWG
items.short_def: The decision right is agreed through a technical working group's terms of reference.
items.long_def: Choose TWG when the decision is made by a technical working group whose authority comes from its own terms of reference rather than a law or decree. This is common in early stages and works where members comply voluntarily, but decisions may not bind programmes, partners or vendors who disagree. The RA notes that a single committee may hold both strategic and operational roles early on, with a roadmap to formalise them as capacity grows.
items.examples: Digital health TWG; interoperability or standards sub-committee; HIS coordination committee

items.label: None
items.short_def: There is no formal basis; the decision happens in practice only.
items.long_def: Choose None when someone does make the decision but nothing written gives them the authority, or when no one makes it at all. Note which applies. Informal arrangements can work while people stay in post but are fragile when staff, funding or leadership change; the RA treats documented decision rights as a precondition for shared infrastructure.
items.examples: A programme manager who maintains the facility list by custom; standards chosen project by project
items.source: RA 3.4.1; RA 3.4.2 (Transparency and accountability); Workshop guidance

items.label: Data protection covers health data
items.short_def: Data protection law applies to health data: how it is collected, used, shared and kept.
items.long_def: This asks whether a law sets rules for personal health data, such as lawful purposes, consent, security, retention and individual rights, and whether a regulator enforces it. The RA expects storage, exchange and access to default to data minimisation and purpose limitation within the applicable law, and asks a national assessment to check that a legal framework for health data exists. Answer for health data specifically: a general privacy law that excludes or is silent on health counts as partial.
items.examples: National data protection act with health data as a sensitive category; health records act; health information privacy code
items.source: RA 2.3 (Principles VIII and X); RA 4.1.2; RA 4.6.2

items.label: Basis for cross-border sharing
items.short_def: A legal basis exists to send health data to other countries, or to accept and rely on theirs.
items.long_def: Cross-border exchange needs explicit legal authority and consent arrangements, plus mutual recognition of identities, credentials and signatures. The RA states that the legal basis and consent arrangements for cross-border processing must be explicit, and favours federated exchange through national gateways over a central store of personal data. Check both directions: sending data out, and relying on documents issued abroad.
items.examples: Bilateral agreement on medical referrals; adequacy or transfer provisions in a data protection act; IHR reporting obligations; participation in WHO GDHCN

items.label: Consent for minors and dependants
items.short_def: Rules exist on who may consent for children and other dependants, and when that changes.
items.long_def: This asks whether law or policy says who can consent on behalf of a child or an adult who cannot decide, and at what age or capacity a young person decides for themselves. The RA leaves these rules to each country but expects systems to support them, for example the Client Registry linking a child's record to a mother or guardian. Without clear rules, systems either over-share or block legitimate access.
items.examples: Age of consent for health data access; guardian access to adolescent records; proxy access for carers

items.label: Procurement conditions
items.short_def: Requirements written into tenders and contracts that systems must meet to be bought.
items.long_def: Procurement is often the most immediate lever: tenders and contracts can require open standards, standard APIs, conformance testing, data portability and the right to move to another supplier. The RA calls for aligning procurement with open standards early, treating conformance as mandatory, and planning replacements at natural transition points. It works only for new purchases and renewals, so pair it with other levers for existing systems.
items.examples: FHIR conformance clause in tenders; data ownership and exit clauses; requirement to use the national client registry

items.label: TWG mandate
