items.short_def: Decisions the technical working group is empowered to make and enforce.
items.long_def: A TWG mandate can be used to agree standards, approve new systems, coordinate partners or set data definitions, within the authority its terms of reference give it. The RA distinguishes strategic from operational governance and expects clear escalation paths when issues exceed operational authority. The lever is strong only if programmes and partners actually follow TWG decisions.
items.examples: TWG approval before a new system connects; agreed national code lists; partner coordination on a shared roadmap

items.label: Conditional financing
items.short_def: Funding released only when agreed conditions, such as standards conformance or reuse of shared components, are met.
items.long_def: Conditional financing links money to architecture: domestic budgets or partner funds flow when a project uses the national registries, meets standards or has a sustainability plan. The RA asks development partners to align with the national architecture rather than build parallel systems, and asks blended financing to carry an explicit transition plan. Ministries of Finance can apply the same conditions to domestic budgets.
items.examples: Results-based loan tranches tied to registry coverage; co-financing conditional on a transition plan; budget approval conditional on architecture review

items.label: Regulation or licensing
items.short_def: Rules that systems or providers must meet in order to operate.
items.long_def: Regulation and licensing can require providers, insurers or software vendors to use national identifiers, report data, connect to shared services or meet security rules as a condition of operating. Unlike procurement, it can reach private providers and existing systems. The RA notes that the legal basis for requiring conformance must exist for this lever to hold.
items.examples: Facility licensing tied to reporting through the national HMIS; insurer accreditation requiring standard claims data; registration of health software

items.label: System certification
items.short_def: Testing systems against national requirements before they are allowed to connect or be used.
items.long_def: Certification checks that a system correctly implements national profiles, terminology and exchange rules, including vendors' claims, before and during procurement. The RA recommends minimum conformance requirements for each component, a shared, open test bed, and considering certification as a condition of procurement approval. It makes standards enforceable rather than advisory.
items.examples: National FHIR conformance test bed; IHE Connectathon-style testing; certified EMR list

items.label: Integration effort
items.short_def: The work to connect systems to each other and to shared services.
items.long_def: Integration includes building interfaces, mapping codes and data, testing and maintaining connections. The RA notes that without shared infrastructure these costs grow much faster than the number of systems, because every programme needs a link to every other, and each update risks breaking them. Integrating legacy systems through standard APIs is usually cheaper in the near term than replacing them.
items.examples: Connecting immunisation and HIV systems to the client registry; mapping local codes to the national terminology

items.label: Devices and connectivity at point of care
items.short_def: Hardware, power and network access where care is actually given.
items.long_def: Shared infrastructure only helps if staff at the point of care can use it, which may need tablets, computers, power and connectivity in clinics and community settings. The RA expects coverage to extend to primary care, community health and low-connectivity settings, and requires key components to support offline operation with later synchronisation. These costs are often large and recurrent (replacement, data plans, maintenance).
items.examples: Tablets for community health workers; solar power for remote clinics; mobile data plans; offline-capable apps
items.source: RA 4.2.2 (Phase 3); RA 3.6.3; Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record, offline operation)

items.label: Training and change management
items.short_def: Preparing staff and changing ways of working so new systems are actually used.
items.long_def: This covers user training, supervision, workflow redesign and communication of benefits, as well as building specialist skills. The RA stresses that changes are sustained only where change management is planned and resourced as deliberately as the technology. It is often underbudgeted because it is spread across programmes.
items.examples: Training of facility staff on a new registry; workflow redesign for referrals; national informatics training programme

items.label: Terminology licensing
items.short_def: Fees for using licensed terminologies such as SNOMED CT.
items.long_def: Some terminologies are free (for example ICD-11 for most uses and LOINC) while SNOMED CT needs a licence: it is free in member countries of SNOMED International, whose membership fee is paid nationally, and otherwise licensed directly. The RA asks countries to confirm their licensing position before adoption and notes SNOMED GPS as a free subset. A regional or pooled arrangement can sometimes reduce cost.
items.examples: SNOMED International membership fee; affiliate licences; national release centre staffing

items.label: Running shared infrastructure
items.short_def: Recurring costs of hosting, maintaining, supporting and governing shared services.
items.long_def: Running costs include hosting, security, upgrades, help desk, data stewardship and governance staff, year after year. The RA warns that systems often fail when operating costs are underestimated, asks that options be judged on whole-of-life cost, and treats financial continuity as a core governance mandate funded through recurrent budget lines. Shared services make these costs visible in one place even when they save money overall.
items.examples: Cloud or data centre hosting; registry data stewards; service desk; annual security audits

items.label: The cost of not doing it once
items.short_def: The cost of several programmes each building and maintaining their own version of the same thing.
items.long_def: This is the hidden cost of fragmentation: duplicate registries, repeated data entry, inconsistent lists and many separate integrations. The RA argues that these costs compound as systems are added, and that pooling investment across programmes turns duplicated spending into lasting national capability. Estimating this cost helps make the case to Ministries of Finance.
items.examples: Separate patient lists in HIV, TB and immunisation systems; several facility lists; health workers filling multiple programme reports

items.label: Domestic budget
items.short_def: Funding from the government's own budget.
items.long_def: Domestic funding can be a recurrent line in the health budget, a contribution from a health coverage scheme, or reinvested efficiency savings. The RA describes a recurrent national budget line as the most predictable basis and a signal of government ownership, and expects a gradual shift from external to domestic financing. Engaging the Ministry of Finance early helps secure it.
items.examples: Recurrent digital health budget line; contribution from a national health insurance scheme; savings from reduced fraud reinvested

items.label: World Bank
items.short_def: Loans, credits or grants from the World Bank Group.
items.long_def: The World Bank lends to and grants funds to governments (through IBRD and IDA), often as health system projects with digital health components, and also funds identity and digital public infrastructure programmes. The RA notes that partner financing works best when aligned to the national architecture and blended with domestic funding under an explicit transition plan.
items.examples: Health system strengthening project with a digital health component; IDA grant or credit; ID4D-supported identity programme

items.label: ADB
items.short_def: Loans, grants or technical assistance from the Asian Development Bank.
items.long_def: ADB finances governments in Asia and the Pacific through loans, grants and technical assistance, including health projects with digital health and health information components. As with other partners, the RA expects such financing to align with the national architecture and to carry a plan for transition to domestic funding.
items.examples: Health sector loan with a digital health component; regional technical assistance grant

items.label: Bilateral or other donor
items.short_def: Funding from another government's aid programme, a foundation or a global health initiative.
items.long_def: This covers bilateral aid agencies, philanthropic foundations and global health initiatives that fund health programmes. The RA notes that donor funding structured around individual programme results has historically driven vertical systems, and asks partners to fund shared components the country has prioritised instead of parallel systems.
items.examples: Bilateral aid programme; global health fund grant with a digital component; philanthropic foundation grant

items.label: Other
items.short_def: Another funding source the team names.
items.long_def: Use this for sources not listed, such as private-sector partnerships, other development banks or regional funds. The RA notes private-sector arrangements can provide hosting or development, provided government keeps ownership of core registries and their data.
items.examples: Public-private partnership for hosting; other multilateral or regional fund

items.label: AeHIN
items.short_def: The Asia eHealth Information Network: a regional peer network of digital health practitioners across Asia and the Pacific.
items.long_def: AeHIN brings together ministry staff, implementers and partners for peer learning, capacity building and convenings on digital health governance, architecture, programme management and standards. Refer a gap here when what is needed is shared learning, regional capacity or a community to develop common approaches.
items.examples: Regional meetings and communities of practice; capacity-building on interoperability and identity

items.label: ADB
items.short_def: The Asian Development Bank: a multilateral development bank financing development in Asia and the Pacific.
items.long_def: ADB provides loans, grants and technical assistance to member governments, including for health systems and digital health. Refer a gap here when it needs investment financing or associated technical assistance.
items.examples: Health sector loans and grants; technical assistance for digital health planning

items.label: World Bank
items.short_def: The World Bank Group: a multilateral development bank providing financing and advice to governments worldwide.
items.long_def: The World Bank finances and advises governments, including on health systems, identity and digital public infrastructure; the RA draws on its definition of DPI. Refer a gap here when it needs large-scale investment financing or policy and analytical support.
items.examples: Health and digital development projects; DPI and identity advisory work

items.label: WHO
items.short_def: The World Health Organization, the UN specialised agency for health, including its regional and country offices.
items.long_def: WHO sets global health norms and provides technical guidance and support to ministries, including in digital health (this RA with ITU, SMART Guidelines, GDHCN). Refer a gap here when it concerns guidance, standards adoption, normative content or technical support.
items.examples: Technical support from WPRO or SEARO; SMART Guidelines adaptation; GDHCN onboarding

items.label: SPC
items.short_def: The Pacific Community: the main intergovernmental scientific and technical organisation for Pacific island countries and territories.
items.long_def: SPC's Public Health Division supports Pacific members on health information, surveillance and laboratory networks. Refer a gap here when it is shared among Pacific island countries and territories and suits regional technical support.
items.examples: Pacific Public Health Surveillance Network; regional health data support

items.label: Other
items.short_def: Another organisation the team names.
items.long_def: Use this for any other partner suited to the gap, such as a bilateral agency, standards body, academic institution or another country. Name the organisation and the kind of help expected.
items.examples: A standards development organisation; a university informatics programme; a peer ministry

items.label: Policy, legislation and regulation
items.short_def: The laws, mandates and decision-making arrangements that set what the health system's shared digital infrastructure is for and who decides.
items.long_def: Strategic governance sets the mission and scope of the shared infrastructure, approves major cross-organisational changes, keeps it financially sustainable across funding cycles, and gives underserved communities a genuine voice. It rests on legal mandates, data-protection law, agreed architecture principles and governance of digital health investment. The RA treats governance as something that comes before technology: countries that agree who decides what, and establish authoritative registries, tend to progress, while those starting from applications tend to fragment. The specific bodies and procedures are a national choice; the RA's examples are illustrative, not prescriptive.
items.examples: Legal mandates for national registries; data-protection law; national digital health strategy and architecture principles; ministerial steering committee holding strategic authority in early-stage countries
items.source: RA 1.4 (Public Governance); RA 2.3 (Principle I Governance); RA 3.4.1-3.4.3, 3.4.7; RA Integrated View

items.label: Cybersecurity, privacy and consent
items.short_def: Protecting health data and giving people control through consent that is specific, can be withdrawn and is tied to a purpose.
items.long_def: The RA treats security and privacy as built-in architectural properties, applying zero-trust principles by default, keeping data confidential in transit and at rest, and containing the damage if any one component is compromised. Consent is the main way people exercise rights over their data: it should be recorded in a common, standards-based form and travel with the data, while the rules on what counts as valid consent remain a matter for national law. Where national trust infrastructure (PKI, digital signatures) or cross-sector consent infrastructure exists, health can build on it; otherwise a health-sector consent capability may be needed. Security levels can be graduated to match each country's capacity and the sensitivity of the data.
items.examples: Zero-trust architecture; encryption; PKI management; HL7 FHIR Consent resource; IHE privacy and consent profiles; consent enforced at the point of data exchange
items.source: RA 1.4 (Security and Privacy); RA 2.3 (Principles VIII and IX); RA Table 2.2; RA Integrated View

items.label: Standards, certification and conformance
items.short_def: Deciding which standards systems must use, and testing and certifying that systems actually meet them.
items.long_def: Because interoperability depends on systems conforming to shared specifications, conformance can be tested, including vendors' claims, before and during procurement. The RA describes testing at two levels: whether systems correctly implement their expected role and standards, and whether a national architecture is well formed and aligned with the reference. Where an exchange matches an IHE transaction, the RA defers to IHE specifications and testing tools. Countries can set minimum conformance requirements for each DPI-H component and may require certification against published profiles as a condition of procurement.
items.examples: National FHIR profiles; SNOMED CT; ICD; LOINC; GS1; open interoperability test beds with validators and simulators; IHE Connectathons; conformance certification against published profiles
items.source: RA 3.6.5; RA 3.7.1-3.7.4; RA 4.3.5; RA 4.4; RA Integrated View

items.label: Semantic governance and stewardship
items.short_def: The people, roles and processes that look after what health data means: terminologies, data models and code maps.
items.long_def: The RA calls this the Semantic Governance Infrastructure (SGI): a cross-cutting governance capability, mainly institutions, roles and workflows rather than software, that keeps the registries, Terminology Service and Logical Information Model Repository accurate and consistent over time. It covers intake of change requests, review and versioned publication, monitoring of quality and use, and distribution to implementers. It also balances global, national and local content, passing global standards down while feeding local needs back up. The RA presents this cross-registry governance layer as something DPI-H adds beyond earlier architectures such as OpenHIE, and advises investing in committees and decision rights before tooling.
items.examples: Curation of reference and local terminologies; logical model versioning; code-system maps; HL7 Unified Terminology Governance (UTG); SNOMED International National Release Centre model; OpenHIE terminology maturity model
items.source: RA 3.4.4; RA 3.4.5 (Figures 3.4.1-3.4.3); Appendix F; RA Integrated View

items.label: Auditability, assurance and accountability
items.short_def: Being able to check who did what with health data and with shared infrastructure, and to report it openly.
items.long_def: The RA makes transparency and accountability a governance principle: decisions on resources, priorities and enforcement should be documented, disclosed and open to review, because accountability without transparency is not accountability. Technically this relies on tamper-evident logs, digital signatures and provenance, so that the origin and integrity of data and documents can be shown. For example, the Lifelong Health Record keeps a full audit log of access, and foundational data exchange provides signed, time-stamped transaction logs. Independent audit and open disclosure let the public and oversight bodies check that the infrastructure is used as intended.
items.examples: Immutable or tamper-evident audit logs; digital signatures; signed and time-stamped exchange logs; break-glass access with full audit trail; independent audit; open disclosure
items.source: RA 3.4.2 (Transparency and accountability); RA 2.3 (Principles IX and X); RA 3.6.3; Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record); RA Integrated View

items.label: AI-enabled intelligence
items.short_def: AI models that many health programmes can share, run under national control and built on trusted, governed data.
items.long_def: This box in the Integrated View covers shared AI capabilities such as risk stratification and climate-health forecasting, used for public health, clinical and secondary-use work. The RA does not define AI as a separate DPI-H component: it stresses that AI depends on the shared data foundations (registries, Terminology Service, LIMR, interoperability and consent), and that clinical AI functions belong to applications and analytics built on that foundation. It favours assistive tools under human oversight, grounding models in authoritative registries so outputs can be traced and audited, and having models call governed services for calculations that must be exact. Some countries are exploring sovereign models hosted under national or regional control.
items.examples: Risk stratification; climate-health forecasting; outbreak forecasting; claims fraud detection; demand forecasting; extracting structured data from scanned documents

items.label: Secondary use
items.short_def: Reusing health data for analysis, research and AI, after it has been de-identified or protected and limited to clear purposes.
items.long_def: Secondary use means using data collected for care for other purposes such as analytics, research, planning, performance and equity reporting, international reporting, or training AI models. The RA's ethics principle requires this to rest on de-identified or privacy-protected data, bound to defined and transparent purposes, and not to harm individuals or groups. The Lifelong Health Record and HMIS are expected to support governed export for secondary use without parallel data collection, under semantic governance. The RA cites the European framework as an example that separates direct-care use from governed secondary use, each with its own access and oversight rules.
items.examples: AI/ML model training; public-good analytics; performance and equity reporting; IHR / IPS reporting; European Health Data Space secondary-use framework
items.source: RA 2.3 (Principle X Ethics); RA 3.6.4; Appendix C (Lifelong Health Record, Health Management Information System); RA Integrated View

items.label: CDS Hooks
items.short_def: A standard way for clinical systems to call decision-support services at the right moment in a health worker's workflow.
items.long_def: CDS Hooks lets a point-of-care system call an external decision-support service at defined moments, such as opening a record or ordering a medicine, and show the returned advice. The RA names it as one of the standard interfaces through which applications call the Computable Decision Support Engine, so decision logic can be maintained centrally without bespoke integration.
items.examples: CDS Hooks specification (cds-hooks.org)
items.source: Appendix C (Computable Decision Support Engine); Appendix D.1

items.label: SMART on FHIR
items.short_def: A standard for launching apps inside clinical systems with secure, authorised access to FHIR data.
items.long_def: SMART on FHIR defines how third-party apps launch from within an electronic record system and obtain authorised access to its FHIR data. The RA lists it with CDS Hooks as an integration pattern for the Computable Decision Support Engine, allowing decision-support apps to run within point-of-care workflows.
items.examples: SMART App Launch

items.label: IDMP / UDI
items.short_def: International identifiers for medicines (ISO IDMP) and for medical devices (Unique Device Identification).
items.long_def: ISO IDMP standards identify medicinal products and their ingredients consistently across regulators, and UDI gives each medical device a unique identifier. The RA lists IDMP-family identifiers among the product standards it references, and the Product Registry can receive data from national IDMP implementations and record device UDIs alongside other product identifiers.
items.examples: ISO IDMP; UDI

items.label: OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0
items.short_def: Standards for signing people in and allowing apps and services to access data only with the right permission.
items.long_def: OAuth 2.0 is a standard for granting applications limited access to data, and OpenID Connect adds a standard way to confirm who a user is. They underpin authorisation patterns such as SMART on FHIR and single sign-on. The RA does not name them directly, but requires that data be accessed and exchanged only between participants whose identity and authorisation can be verified, drawing on foundational identity and trust services.

items.label: Hybrid / sovereign cloud
items.short_def: Where systems run: public cloud, private cloud or on-premise hosting, chosen to respect national rules on where data is kept.
items.long_def: This layer covers hosting models and the platforms used to run DPI-H components, such as containers, Kubernetes and edge computing for remote sites. The RA is technology-neutral and does not prescribe a hosting model, but its autonomy and sovereignty principle says countries should keep core health infrastructure under national control and not depend on outside actors to keep it running.
items.examples: Public, private and on-premise cloud; data residency controls; containers; Kubernetes; edge computing
items.source: RA Integrated View; RA 1.4 (Autonomy and Sovereignty); RA 3.5.1 (technology-neutral)

items.label: AI / ML platform
items.short_def: The tools to build, run and monitor AI models responsibly and under national control.
items.long_def: An AI/ML platform includes a model registry, MLOps pipelines, bias monitoring and explainability tools. The RA stresses evaluating models against representative cases before and during use, monitoring drift, and attention to bias and equity. It also advises keeping the ability to swap one model for another to avoid lock-in, noting some countries are exploring sovereign models hosted under national or regional control.
items.examples: Model registry; MLOps; bias monitoring; explainability; evaluations (evals); drift monitoring

items.label: Security and trust operations
items.short_def: The day-to-day work of watching for, preventing and responding to security threats.
items.long_def: Security and trust operations include security monitoring and automated response (SIEM/SOAR), identity and access management, multi-factor authentication, hardware security modules for protecting keys, and encryption at rest and in transit. These put into practice the RA's trust and security principle: verifying identity and authorisation, protecting confidentiality, and containing any compromise. The RA leaves the specific controls to each country's security policy.
items.examples: SIEM / SOAR; identity and access management (IAM); MFA; HSM; encryption at rest and in transit
items.source: RA Integrated View; RA 1.4 (Security and Privacy); RA 2.3 (Principle IX)

items.label: Data platform
items.short_def: The technical platform where data from many sources is brought together, cleaned and made ready for analysis.
items.long_def: A data platform includes a data lakehouse or warehouse, data pipelines (ETL/ELT), master data management and privacy-preserving computation. It supports the HMIS, surveillance and governed secondary use. The RA's ethics principle requires data used for analytics, research or AI to be de-identified or privacy-protected and limited to defined purposes.
items.examples: Lakehouse / data warehouse; ETL / ELT pipelines; master data management (MDM); privacy-preserving compute

items.label: Observability, network and DevSecOps
items.short_def: Keeping systems connected, reliable, monitored and safely updated, without being locked into one vendor.
items.long_def: This covers network connectivity, observability (logs, metrics and traces), reliability engineering, DevSecOps and infrastructure as code, and vendor-neutral procurement. It supports the RA's operational governance responsibilities for service levels, incident management and safe release and change management. The RA also encourages aligning procurement with open standards and conformance requirements to avoid lock-in.
items.examples: Logs, metrics and traces; site reliability engineering; infrastructure as code; DevSecOps; vendor-neutral procurement

items.label: Standards mandated in policy
items.short_def: Policy that names the standards systems must use.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Policy names the required standards, with incentives or consequences attached. Voluntary standards are adopted unevenly; a mandate with incentives or consequences is what moves vendors and programmes.

items.label: National core FHIR implementation guide
items.short_def: A national guide that profiles FHIR for local use, so systems implement it the same way.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Published, and approved through the TWG. FHIR alone leaves many choices open; a national implementation guide fixes them so systems built by different vendors actually work together.
items.examples: National FHIR core IGs (e.g. AU Core); IPS IG

items.label: Terminology service with a change process
items.short_def: A live national service that hosts the code systems and value sets systems use.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Live national terminology server, with change requests, versioning and notice to system owners. Systems stay consistent only if they draw codes from one maintained source and are told when it changes.

items.label: Testing before go-live
items.short_def: A requirement that systems prove they conform before they connect or go live.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Systems must pass a connectathon or sandbox test before go-live or certification. Testing catches non-conformance early, when it is cheap to fix, instead of after systems are in use.
items.examples: IHE Connectathons; national FHIR test sandboxes

items.label: Trained national team
items.short_def: In-country people with the skills to run and evolve the architecture.
items.long_def: **Done means:** A named in-country team or existing capability handles architecture, FHIR IG authoring and terminology mapping without outside help. Without national skills, every change depends on consultants and the infrastructure stalls when projects end.

items.label: National ownership of training & sandbox
items.short_def: A national institution that trains others and hosts the shared test environment.
items.long_def: **Done means:** A national institution runs training-of-trainers and hosts the test environment. National ownership keeps skills and testing available after partner projects finish.

items.label: Progress measured
items.short_def: Regular, structured measurement of digital health maturity, turned into action.
items.long_def: **Done means:** Maturity assessment done in the last 3 years and turned into a roadmap, with indicators tracked (e.g. Global Digital Health Monitor). Measuring progress shows whether investments are working and where to focus next.
items.examples: Global Digital Health Monitor (GDHM)

items.label: Buddies
items.short_def: Supporting experts who sit with a country team: they ask questions and explain, but the country decides.
items.long_def: Buddies come from partner organisations, technical agencies, standards bodies or other countries. They help the team work through the worksheet: they explain terms, share examples from elsewhere, and ask questions that test the team's answers. They don't answer for the country: every answer is the country team's own. Record each buddy's name and organisation only.
items.examples: A standards expert explaining FHIR; an adviser from SPC or WHO; a peer from a country that has already built a client registry

glossary.definition: Digital Public Infrastructure: shared digital systems that are secure and interoperable, can be built on open standards, and deliver equitable access to public and private services at societal scale under applicable legal frameworks (G20 description). Its value comes from being reusable across sectors so that others can build on it, rather than from any single system. The RA treats identity, payments and data exchange as the typical foundational DPI.

Foundational DPI: the whole-of-government systems for identity, payments and data exchange that any sector can use. The RA says health should build on them where they exist, are trusted and are accessible, and add health-specific components only where they fall short. Where they are absent, health may need interim capabilities designed to align with them later.

Digital Public Infrastructure for Health: digital resources, both systems and specifications, built as a shared means for fulfilling multiple health agency functions. They build on foundational DPI, are interoperable, reusable, publicly governed and based on open standards. DPI-H is distinct from programme-specific tools and point-of-service applications, which consume it.

A technology-neutral blueprint of the common building blocks, relationships and design principles of a technical environment, so countries do not start from a blank page. The DPI-H RA traces each component back to the health goals it serves, using TOGAF and ArchiMate methods. It is an adaptive framework, not a list of products to procure.

Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure: the governed, interoperable, standards-based state countries work towards, in which shared foundations are reused rather than duplicated. It is a direction of travel, not a certification; progress is shown by authoritative registries reused across programmes, governed standards-based exchange and actively managed data quality. Its minimum core is the core registries, the Lifelong Health Record, terminology and the means to exchange data between them.

A deployable, modular piece of software that provides a defined set of functions, holds the data it manages, and exposes both through services. In the RA, DPI-H components (such as registries) are shared infrastructure reusable across many domains, while functional applications serve one programme or institution. Naming a component is not a prescription to buy a specific product.

An end-user system used by people directly involved in care, such as an EMR, a community health worker app, a pharmacy system or a patient app. These consume DPI-H (for example by looking up the client registry or sending data to the health record) but are not themselves DPI-H, so the RA does not specify their functions.

A high-level ability the health system has or needs to achieve its goals, described independently of how it is implemented. In the RA, goals map to capabilities, capabilities to application services, and services to the components that deliver them, so that every component can be traced back to a goal.

A specific, real situation in which a health goal is delivered: who is involved, what happens and what outcome changes. In this framework it is the unit of the use-case dimension, completed once per priority use case. The RA recommends anchoring early implementation on a few high-value use cases within two to three priority goals.

This framework's scale for rating component and enabler status, from 0 (nothing in place) to 4 (mature). It is a workshop tool; the RA itself does not define numbered levels but describes observable markers of progress and recommends using recognised readiness and governance maturity assessments. See Maturity_Scales for each level's description.

One of four starting positions the RA describes: building from the ground up, integrating existing systems, upgrading existing infrastructure, and scaling and deepening. Each implies a different priority, from setting governance before buying technology, to connecting existing systems, to fixing openness and lock-in, to moving towards business services and domestic financing. Countries pick the one closest to their reality and adapt the phased approach accordingly.

The standards-based ability of different information systems to communicate, exchange data and use what they receive with the same meaning. The RA treats it as a property of the whole architecture rather than a single component, built from shared content standards, terminology, information models and agreed exchange patterns. It can be tested through conformance.

The function that connects systems so they can exchange health data securely, authenticating and auditing participants and routing messages. The RA treats mediation as a role rather than one product: it may be a central service bus, distributed access points, gateways, direct standards-based connections or a mix. Where government-wide data exchange exists, health should reuse it for transport and add health-specific content standards.

Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources: the HL7 standard for exchanging health data as modular resources over web APIs. The RA names FHIR as the primary framework for health data exchange and the recommended basis for national profiles and implementation guides. National profiles constrain FHIR for local use and can be tested for conformance.

International Patient Summary: an internationally agreed minimum set of a person's key health information (such as problems, medicines, allergies and immunisations) designed to be understood across systems and borders. It is published as an HL7 FHIR implementation guide and an ISO standard. The RA names it as the shared specification on which cross-border care exchange depends.

A comprehensive clinical terminology for coding diagnoses, findings, procedures and other clinical facts consistently. It is free to use in member countries of SNOMED International and otherwise licensed directly; SNOMED GPS is a freely available subset. The RA expects it to be hosted and governed through the national Terminology Service.
glossary.source: RA Glossary; RA 2.2.2 (footnote); Appendix C (Terminology Service)

glossary.definition: LOINC is a common set of codes and names for laboratory tests, observations and documents. ICD-11 is WHO's International Classification of Diseases, used for mortality and morbidity statistics, reporting and increasingly for clinical recording. The RA lists both, with SNOMED CT, among the terminologies that give data consistent meaning across systems and borders.

Logical Information Model Repository: the national home for data models that define what a record contains and how it is structured, while the Terminology Service defines what codes mean. It keeps information models consistent across systems and limits uncontrolled local variation. The RA treats it as an enabler that can be built up as maturity grows rather than part of the minimum foundation.
glossary.source: RA 2.2.1 (Table 2.2); RA 3.5.3; Appendix C (LIMR); Bootcamp glossary

glossary.definition: Pacific Clinical Data for Interoperability: an agreed Pacific minimum clinical dataset, modelled in openEHR, intended to give Pacific systems a common core of clinical data. It is an example of a regional artefact that countries can adopt and adapt instead of each defining their own. It is not referenced in the RA.

WHO Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, Testable guidelines: reusable digital packages of WHO recommendations, from narrative guidance through digital adaptation kits to computable content that decision-support systems can run. The RA counts them as open content and as the source of logic for the Clinical Decision Support Engine. Not to be confused with SMART on FHIR.

The governance, mainly people, roles and processes rather than software, that keeps terminology, data models and registry content accurate and consistent over time. It covers change requests, review, versioned publication, quality monitoring and distribution to implementers, balancing global, national and local content. The RA calls it the Semantic Governance Infrastructure and advises investing in it alongside the tools it governs.

WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network: an openly governed trust network through which participating authorities verify that health documents issued by each other are genuine and unaltered, using shared public key infrastructure. Personal data stays with the issuer; the network shares only the means to verify. One trust mechanism serves many document types, such as vaccination certificates and patient summaries.

The agreed rules, identities, credentials, signatures and consent arrangements that let organisations rely on each other's systems and data. The RA asks for graduated levels of assurance matched to context, building on national trust infrastructure where it exists, and for an explicit cross-jurisdiction trust framework for cross-border exchange.

The part of this framework's assessment completed once per country: national context, the enabling environment (identity, consent, exchange, trust, payments, legal framework) and the inventory of DPI-H components. It reflects the RA's first assessment questions about what exists and the state of foundational DPI and governance.

The part of this framework's assessment completed for each priority use case: what the use case needs, the pathway to deliver it and whether it is a candidate for regional work. It reflects the RA's advice to anchor implementation on specific high-value use cases within priority goals.
